## The gas-phase gap

The *fundamental gap* of a molecule is the difference between its ionization potential and
electron affinity,

$$
E_g = \mathrm{IP} - \mathrm{EA}.
$$ {#eq-gap}

Kohn–Sham eigenvalues from semilocal density functionals underestimate $E_g$ substantially. Many-body
perturbation theory in the GW approximation fixes this by adding a self-energy correction to each
level [@Hedin1965; @Hybertsen1986]:

$$
E_n^{\mathrm{QP}} = \varepsilon_n^{\mathrm{KS}}
  + \left\langle \psi_n \middle| \Sigma\!\left(E_n^{\mathrm{QP}}\right) - V_{\mathrm{xc}} \middle| \psi_n \right\rangle .
$$ {#eq-qp}

In practice @eq-qp is usually solved to first order, which introduces a renormalization
factor $Z_n$.[^z]

[^z]: $Z_n = \left(1 - \partial \Sigma / \partial E \right)^{-1}$, evaluated at the Kohn–Sham energy. Typical values are 0.7–0.9.

## What the metal does

When an electron is added to or removed from an adsorbed molecule, conduction electrons in the metal
rearrange to screen the extra charge. Classically, a point charge $q$ at distance $z$ from a
perfect conductor feels its image, which lowers its energy by

::: {.column-margin}
$z$ is measured from the metal's *image plane*, which sits roughly 1 Å outside the top atomic layer.
:::

$$
\Delta E(z) = -\frac{q^2}{16\pi\varepsilon_0 z} \approx -\frac{3.6\ \mathrm{eV\,Å}}{z}.
$$ {#eq-image}

Both the added electron and the added hole are stabilised by @eq-image, so the occupied level moves
up, the unoccupied level moves down, and the gap closes by twice that amount. @Neaton2006 showed that
GW calculations on benzene adsorbed on graphite capture exactly this renormalization, which is absent from
the Kohn–Sham gap.

```{python}
#| label: fig-image-charge
#| fig-cap: "Gap reduction from the classical image-charge model, $2|\\Delta E(z)|$ from @eq-image, as a function of the molecule–image-plane distance."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the plotting code"
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

K = 14.3996  # e^2 / (4 pi eps0) in eV·Å
z = np.linspace(2.0, 10.0, 200)          # Å
gap_reduction = 2 * K / (4 * z)          # eV, electron + hole images

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.4))
ax.plot(z, gap_reduction, color="#0066cc", lw=2)
ax.set_xlabel("distance from image plane, z (Å)")
ax.set_ylabel("gap reduction (eV)")
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
ax.grid(alpha=0.25)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@fig-image-charge shows why the effect matters: at a typical physisorption distance of 3–4 Å the
predicted gap reduction is about 2 eV, comparable to the error that GW corrects in the first place.

## How the methods compare

| Method | Captures substrate screening? | Cost for a 500-atom interface |
|:-------|:-----------------------------:|:------------------------------|
| Kohn–Sham DFT (semilocal) | No | Low |
| Full GW on the interface | Yes | Very high |
| Substrate-screening GW | Yes | Moderate |
| Generalized substrate-screening GW | Yes, including covalent bonds | Moderate |

: Approaches to quasiparticle levels at interfaces. {#tbl-methods}

@tbl-methods summarises the trade-off. Treating the whole interface at the GW level is accurate but
expensive, so we compute the substrate's polarizability separately and embed it. The generalized
version also handles covalently bonded interfaces such as thiolates on gold [@FL24], and related
many-body treatments apply to quantum-dot assemblies [@AFL22].

::: {.callout-note}
## Rule of thumb
If your molecule sits within about 5 Å of a metal, expect its gap to shrink by 1–2 eV relative to
the gas phase. A calculation that ignores the substrate will overestimate the gap.
:::

> The image-charge model is a guide, not a substitute: it ignores the molecule's own polarizability,
> the finite size of the charge distribution and chemical bonding to the surface.

## Reproducing this

The figure above is generated when the page renders. To run a quick G₀W₀ calculation yourself, a
typical sequence with Quantum ESPRESSO and WEST looks like this:

```bash
pw.x    -i pw.in    > pw.out     # ground state
wstat.x -i wstat.in > wstat.out  # dielectric screening
wfreq.x -i wfreq.in > wfreq.out  # quasiparticle corrections
```
